subject: Variance in the estimate of cluster size

messages.author: 29b3187023d3ad5b
messages.subject: Variance in the estimate of cluster size
parts:
Hi everyone,
I used program Distance to estimate detection probability and density of nest trees utilized by my study species in a forested survey area, post-stratified on a 3-factor categorical covariate representing forest age classes. My study species utilizes several nest trees per individual home range, and their home ranges don't overlap. There is an independent publication where the authors estimated the mean number of nest trees per home range, and I'd like to incorporate their results and estimate the density of individual home ranges in my study area. I can use the cluster function for this by treating each nest tree as a fraction of a home range, but the mean number of nest trees per home range (from the other publication) had a significant SD and I need to somehow incorporate this additional variance. Can anybody suggest a method to incorporate the SD associated with the cluster size estimate into my analysis? Thank you!

Chad

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Variance in the estimate of cluster size
parts:
Chad

The apt analogy is not cluster size, but rather  a cue-counting survey; with trees being the equivalent of cues.  You know multiple trees are used by an individual; hence you want to multiply  your tree density estimate by 1/(trees per individual) to estimate individuals per area.  This is equivalent to the adjustment of cue density into animal density with the conversion factor of cue rate.

Another analogy would be dung surveys; you measure density of something created by the animal, rather than the animal itself.  Dung surveys are more complicated that what you are doing because of the need to estimate creation and disappearance rates.

Essentially you can use the delta method approximation, based upon "squared CVs add".  Assume "TD" is your estimate of tree density and "UT" is your estimate of used trees (per individual), and you wish to estimate precision of animal density "A":

​

If you want se(A), you can obtain this by

se(A) = cv(A) * A

For more details, look into the distance sampling literature under the term "indirect surveys"; e.g. Section 9.3 & 9.4 of Buckland et al. (2015).
